title: Light sources: why the Moon is not one, and what darkness is

summary.text: The Moon looks like a lamp in the night sky, but it makes no light at all. It is a ball of grey rock, and the light we see is sunlight bouncing off it. In a dark room, your child makes a paper Moon: a sheet of white paper that lights up a picture only while a torch shines on it. They also find that darkness is not a thing that comes in. It is simply what we see where no light is arriving.
summary.art: A night sky with a bright Moon over a city of flats, and a thin dotted line drawn from the Sun, below the edge of the Earth, up to the Moon and down to a girl's window.

intro.hook: On a full-Moon night, the Moon can be bright enough to light up a terrace. So is the Moon a light source, like a lamp?
intro.text: The Moon looks like a big lamp in the sky. But the Moon is a ball of rock, and rock makes no light. So where does the Moon's light come from? And what is the dark that comes back when a cloud covers the Moon? In this unit you make a paper Moon in a dark room, and find out.
intro.art: A girl and her grandmother on the terrace of a flat at night, looking up at a bright full Moon, with their shadows on the floor.

outcomes: By the end I can say what a light source is, and name five light sources.
By the end I can explain that the Moon is not a light source: it shines with sunlight that bounces off it.
By the end I can show that light bouncing off a white thing can light up something else, and that white things send back more light than black things.
By the end I can explain that darkness is what we see where no light is arriving, and that dark does not move or spread.
By the end I can do a fair test by changing only one thing, and count what I see.
By the end I can say why I must never look straight at the Sun.

terms.meaning: A light source is a thing that makes its own light.
terms.example: The Sun, a diya flame, a tube light and a switched-on torch are light sources. The Moon is not.
terms.art: The Sun, a diya flame, a tube light and a torch in a row, each with short rays, and a grey Moon at the end with no rays.

terms.meaning: When light reflects, it bounces off a thing and travels on. Light that reflects off a thing lets us see that thing.
terms.example: Sunlight reflects off the Moon and comes to our eyes. Torch light reflects off a white wall and lights up the room.
terms.art: Arrows of light going from a torch to a white wall, and bouncing off the wall towards a child's eyes.

terms.meaning: Moonlight is sunlight that has reflected off the Moon and come down to the Earth.
terms.example: On a full-Moon night, moonlight can make soft shadows on a terrace floor.
terms.art: A terrace at night with a soft shadow of a potted tulsi, and the bright Moon above.

terms.meaning: Darkness is what we see where no light, or very little light, is arriving. It is the absence of light.
terms.example: Inside a shut cupboard it is dark, because no light can get in.
terms.art: A steel cupboard with its door shut, drawn black inside, and the same cupboard with the door open and light pouring in.

terms.meaning: Dim means there is only a little light. Things are hard to see, but not gone.
terms.example: A room lit only by a phone screen is dim.
terms.art: A room lit only by a glowing phone, with toys on a shelf drawn faint and grey.

terms.meaning: A fair test is a test where we change only one thing and keep everything else the same. Then we know what made the difference.
terms.example: In the Paper Moon test, we change only the paper. The torch, the room and the pictures stay the same.
terms.art: Three sheets of paper in a row, white, grey and black, with the same torch and the same picture card beside each.

explanations.concept: The Moon is not a light source
explanations.definition: The Moon makes no light of its own. It is a ball of rock, and it shines because sunlight reflects off it.
explanations.description: In the Paper Moon test, the white paper made no light. It only sent on the torch's light. The Moon does the same with the Sun's light. The side of the Moon that faces the Sun is bright, and the side that faces away is dark.
examples: In the Paper Moon test, the white paper lit the pictures only while the torch was on.
The bright side of the Moon always faces the Sun.
Astronauts who walked on the Moon found grey rock and dust, not fire or lamps.
explanations.context: This card says where the Moon's light comes from.
explanations.art: The Sun on the left, the Moon in the middle with only its left half lit, and the Earth on the right, with arrows of light from the Sun to the Moon and on to the Earth.

explanations.concept: White things reflect more light than black things
explanations.definition: A white thing reflects most of the light that falls on it. A black thing takes in most of the light and reflects very little.
explanations.description: In the Paper Moon test, the white paper lit up many pictures, and the black cloth lit up few or none. Both got the same torch light. The white paper sent most of it on to the pictures. The black cloth took in most of it and sent very little on.
examples: White paper lit up more pictures than black cloth in the Paper Moon test.
A white kolam on a dark doorstep is easy to see at dusk.
Traffic police in many cities wear white or bright reflective stripes, so drivers see them at night.
explanations.context: This card says why white paper made the best paper Moon.
explanations.art: A torch shining on a white sheet with many arrows bouncing off, and the same torch shining on a black cloth with only one small arrow bouncing off.

explanations.concept: Darkness is the absence of light
explanations.definition: Darkness is not a thing of its own. It is what we see where no light is arriving.
explanations.description: In the Door Test, light from the lit hall came into the dark room, but no dark went out into the hall. Light travels out from a light source, but dark does not travel, because there is nothing there to travel. Thinkers in India argued about this long ago, and their views are below.
examples: When the door opened, the light came in, and no dark came out.
When a cloud covers the Moon, the terrace goes dark because the moonlight stops arriving.
Deep in the sea, below about one kilometre, no sunlight reaches, and the water is completely dark.

perspectives.explanation: Darkness is only the absence of light. It is not a thing of its own. This is what scientists say today.

perspectives.who: Jain thinkers, in the Tattvartha Sutra, India
perspectives.explanation: The Tattvartha Sutra counts darkness and shadow among the forms that matter can take. In this view, darkness is something real, not just nothing.

explanations.context: This card says what darkness is.
explanations.art: A bathroom door half open, a wide band of yellow light coming in from a bright hall and lying across the dark floor.

explanations.definition: The Moon reflects only about one tenth of the sunlight that falls on it. It looks bright because sunlight is very strong and the night sky around it is dark.
explanations.description: Moon rock is dark grey, about as dark as an old tar road. It sends back only about one tenth of the sunlight that lands on it. Sunlight is so strong that this is still enough to light a terrace. The Moon looks bright because the sky around it is black; in the day, the same Moon looks pale because the sky is bright too.
examples: In the Paper Moon test, even the grey newspaper lit up some pictures.
In the daytime, the Moon looks pale white against the blue sky.
Moon rock is about as dark as an old tar road.
explanations.context: This card says how a grey Moon can light up the night.
explanations.art: A lump of dark grey rock in an astronaut's gloved hand, and behind it the bright full Moon in a black sky.

agreed.text: The Moon makes no light of its own. It shines with reflected sunlight.
agreed.evidence: The bright side of the Moon always faces the Sun. Astronauts brought back Moon rock in 1969 and after, and it is grey and gives no light.

agreed.text: Darkness is the absence of light.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can see that light spreads into a dark room through an open door, but dark never spreads into a lit room.

agreed.text: White things reflect more light than black things.
agreed.evidence: In the Paper Moon test, white paper lit up more pictures than black cloth, with the same torch.

agreed.text: Looking straight at the Sun can hurt your eyes for ever.
agreed.evidence: Eye doctors see damage in people who looked at the Sun, for example during eclipses.

challenging.claim: The Moon makes its own light, like a lamp.
challenging.who: A common idea among children, and in many old stories
challenging.for: The Moon looks bright and lights up the night.
challenging.against: The bright side always faces the Sun. Moon rock is grey and makes no light. In the Paper Moon test, the paper went dark the moment the torch went off.
challenging.context: This card is about the Moon's light.

challenging.claim: Darkness is a real thing, not just missing light.
challenging.who: Jain thinkers, in the Tattvartha Sutra, and some other old schools of thought
challenging.for: We can see darkness and point to it. A shadow has a shape and moves with us.
challenging.against: Physicists find nothing in a dark place that is not also in a lit one, except the light. When light comes in, nothing is pushed out.
challenging.context: This card is about what darkness is.

challenging.claim: If you wait long enough in total darkness, your eyes get used to it and you can see.
challenging.for: In a dim room, you see more and more after a few minutes.
challenging.against: Eyes get used to dim light, not to no light. In a room with no light at all, nothing can come to your eyes, however long you wait.
challenging.context: This card is about waiting in the dark.

big_questions.q: On a moonlit night, is the Moon lighting your floor, or is the Sun?
big_questions.hint: Where did the light start? Where did it bounce? Can both answers be true?

big_questions.q: The Moon sends back only about one tenth of the sunlight that falls on it. Where does the rest go?
big_questions.hint: Think of a black cloth in the sun. What happens to the light it takes in?

big_questions.q: Is darkness something, or nothing? Could you catch some darkness in a jar?
big_questions.hint: What would happen the moment you opened the jar in a lit room?

big_questions.q: We see the Moon only because sunlight bounces off it. Do we see most things only because light bounces off them?
big_questions.hint: Look around the room. Which things make their own light? Which only send light on?

story.title: The Night the Moon Lit the Terrace
story.note: Paati means grandmother in Tamil. Pongal is the harvest festival of Tamil Nadu, in January. Kavya, Arjun, Amma and Paati are made up.
text: Kavya was seven. She lived on the fourth floor of a block of flats in Madurai, with her Amma, her Paati and her cousin Arjun, who was five and had come to stay for Pongal.
One evening the power went off. The fans slowed down. The tube lights went out. Everything was black.
"I can't see anything!" said Arjun.
"Come up to the terrace," said Paati. "Tonight is a full-Moon night."

They climbed the stairs slowly, holding the rail. Paati opened the terrace door, and there it was: a huge round Moon, low over the rooftops. The whole terrace was silver. Kavya could see the water tank, the clothes line and the pots of tulsi and jasmine. She could even see her own shadow, soft and grey on the floor.
"The Moon is a big lamp," said Arjun. "It switched on because the power went off."
Kavya laughed. "The Moon doesn't have a switch!"
"Then where does the light come from?" asked Arjun. Kavya opened her mouth, and then closed it again. She did not know.
Paati sat down on the low wall. She took a steel plate out of her bag, the one she used for her betel leaves. She held it up. In the moonlight, it shone.
"Is my plate a lamp?" she asked.
"No," said Arjun. "It is a plate."
"Then why is it shining?"
Arjun thought. "Because the Moon is shining on it."

"Yes," said Paati. "My plate has no light of its own. It only sends on the light that falls on it. The Moon is like my plate, only much, much bigger. The Moon is a ball of grey rock. It sends on the light that falls on it from the Sun."
"But the Sun has gone down," said Kavya. "It's night."

"It is night here," said Paati. "The Sun is still shining. It is shining on the other side of the Earth, where children in America are eating breakfast. The Earth is in the way, so its light does not reach us. But the Moon is high up in the sky, above the edge of the Earth. The sunlight still reaches the Moon, and bounces down to us."
Kavya looked at her shadow on the terrace floor. "So this light came from the Sun?"
"All of it," said Paati. "It left the Sun about eight minutes ago. It flew to the Moon, bounced off the grey rock, and landed on your face."
Just then, a big cloud slid over the Moon. The terrace went dark. Kavya could not see the water tank any more. She could hardly see Paati.
"The dark came back!" said Arjun. "Where did it come from?"
Kavya thought about the steel plate. She thought about the cloud. "The dark didn't come from anywhere," she said slowly. "The cloud is blocking the moonlight. The light stopped coming. That's all."
"So what is the dark?" asked Arjun.
"It's just where the light isn't," said Kavya.
Paati smiled in the dark. "Watch," she said.
The cloud slid on. The moonlight came back, all at once, over the whole terrace. Arjun clapped.
"See?" said Kavya. "The dark didn't go anywhere. The light came back, and there was nowhere left for it to be dark."
Down below, the tube lights flickered on in the flats around them. The fans in the stairway started to whirr. Amma called them for dinner.
On the way down, Arjun stopped at a window and looked back at the Moon. "Thank you, Sun," he whispered. Kavya heard him, and grinned.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Kavya works out two things. The moonlight on the terrace is sunlight that bounced off the Moon, so the Sun is still lighting them at night. And when the cloud covers the Moon, nothing dark arrives: the light simply stops arriving.
ask: Paati's steel plate shone in the moonlight. Was the plate a light source? Why not?
Where was the Sun while Kavya stood in the moonlight?
When the cloud covered the Moon, where did the dark come from?
Why did Arjun say thank you to the Sun, and not to the Moon?
art: A flat at night with the power just gone, a girl and a small boy standing in the dark hall, and a grandmother holding the boy's hand.
A terrace in Madurai lit silver by a huge full Moon, with a water tank, a clothes line, tulsi and jasmine pots and the children's soft shadows.
A grandmother on the terrace wall holding up a shining steel plate, and the two children looking at it.
A dark terrace with a cloud covering the Moon, the children's faces hardly visible, and then the Moon coming out again.

experiments.title: The Paper Moon Test: can bounced light help you see?
experiments.context: In this experiment you make a paper Moon in a dark room. A torch shines on a sheet of paper, and you count how many pictures the bounced light lets you see. Then you try different papers.
experiments.question: In a dark room, which sheet sends the most torch light on to a picture card: white paper, newspaper, black cloth or kitchen foil?
experiments.predict: Which sheet will let you see the most pictures in the dark? Which will let you see the fewest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same torch, the same dark room and the same picture card every time. The torch and the card stay in the same places. We change only the sheet that the torch shines on. We count for the same time, ten seconds, each time.
results_table: My guess: how many pictures will I see?

materials.item: a torch (a phone torch works too)
a picture card: a white sheet with 6 pictures drawn with a thick black pen, from as big as your hand to as small as a coin (a fish, a star, a house, a flower, a kite and a cup)
a thick book, to stand up as a wall
a sheet of white paper
a sheet of newspaper
a black cloth, such as a black T-shirt or dupatta
a piece of kitchen foil, about the size of a notebook
a ruler or a 30 cm scale

schedule.what: In a dark room, shine a torch on four different sheets, and count how many pictures each one lets you see.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar for each sheet: as many boxes as pictures you saw.

setup.art: A picture card with six bold black pen drawings (fish, star, house, flower, kite, cup) next to a white sheet, a newspaper, a black T-shirt and a piece of foil.
setup.caption: 1. Draw six pictures with a thick pen, from big to small. Gather four sheets.

setup.art: A dark bathroom floor seen from above: a torch lying flat pointing at a white sheet held up by a grown-up one ruler away, a picture card standing beside the torch facing the sheet, and a book standing between the torch's front and the card.
setup.caption: 2. The torch shines on the sheet. The book stops it shining on the card.

setup.art: A girl crouching in the dark, looking at the picture card, which is softly lit by light bouncing off the white sheet, counting on her fingers.
setup.caption: 3. Count the pictures you can see. Then change the sheet.

setup.art: The same scene with the torch switched off and everything black, the girl's eyes wide.
setup.caption: 4. Last, switch the torch off. What can you see now?

flow.do: 1. Draw six pictures on a white sheet with a thick black pen. Make them go from big to small. 2. Show your child the four sheets. 3. Let them feel each one.
flow.say: Here are four sheets: white paper, newspaper, black cloth and shiny foil. Soon we will shine a torch on each one in the dark.
flow.kid: Look at the four sheets. Feel each one. Which one looks brightest?

flow.do: Ask your child to guess, for each sheet, how many of the six pictures they will see. Write the guesses in the table.
flow.say: In the dark, we shine the torch only on the sheet, never on the pictures. How many pictures will you see with each sheet? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess how many pictures you will see with each sheet. Why?

ask.q: Why did you guess that number for the foil?
good: It is shiny, so it will send lots of light.
It is like a mirror, so the light might go somewhere else.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine. Many children expect the shiny foil to win. Don't say what will happen.

flow.do: 1. In the darkest room you have at night, lay the torch flat on the floor. 2. Hold the white sheet up, one ruler length in front of the torch, with its face straight to the torch. 3. Stand the card beside the torch, facing the sheet. 4. Stand the book between the torch's front and the card.
flow.say: The torch shines on the white paper. The book stops the torch shining straight on the pictures. Now let's switch off the room light and wait for one minute.
flow.kid: Help set it up. Then the room light goes off. Wait one minute with me.
flow.parent: You hold the sheet. A bathroom with the door shut works well. If light comes under the door, lay a towel along the gap. Check with the room light on that the torch beam does not land on the card itself. Keep every sheet in the same place, flat and straight to the torch.

flow.do: 1. Switch the torch on. 2. Count to ten while your child looks at the card. 3. Your child says how many pictures they can name, big ones and small ones. 4. Write it down. 5. Do the same with the newspaper, the black cloth and the foil, in the same place.
flow.say: Look at the card. Count the pictures you can see. Now let's change the sheet. Same torch, same card, same place. How many now?
flow.kid: Look at the card. How many pictures can you see? Now try the next sheet.

ask.q: Which sheet showed the most pictures?
good: The white paper.
The one that sent the most light on to the card.

flow.parent: In dim light we lose the small pictures first. White paper usually shows most of the six, newspaper fewer, and black cloth few or none. Foil is the surprise. Held flat and straight to the torch, it works like a mirror and sends the beam straight back, so the card may stay dark. Crumple it a little and flatten it again, and it spreads the light and lights the card better. Say what you really saw, even if it is odd.

flow.do: Put the white paper back. Then switch the torch off. Wait ten seconds.
flow.say: The white paper made the pictures visible. Now I am switching the torch off. Is the paper still lighting the pictures?
flow.kid: The torch goes off. Can the white paper still light the pictures?

ask.q: What happened when the torch went off?
good: It all went dark.
The paper stopped lighting the pictures straight away.

flow.do: Switch the room light on. Look at the table together. Ask your child what they think, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Which sheet helped you see the most? Why do you think so? Did the white paper make any light of its own?
flow.kid: Which sheet helped most? Did the paper make its own light? How do you know?

ask.q: What does the paper do with the torch's light?
good: It bounces it on to the pictures.
It sends the light on, but makes none.

ask.q: How is the white paper like the Moon?
good: The Moon bounces the Sun's light to us.
The Moon makes no light of its own, like the paper.

check.q: Revathi, a girl in Kochi, shines a torch on white paper in a dark room. The paper lights up her drawing. Then she switches the torch off. What happens?
options: The paper keeps glowing for a minute
check.why: The paper makes no light of its own. It only sends on the torch's light. When the torch goes off, there is no light to send on. The Moon is the same: it shines only with the Sun's light.

experiments.title: The Blackest Black: a hole in a box
experiments.context: In this experiment you make a small hole in a box covered with black paper. Then you look closely: which is darker, the black paper or the hole?
experiments.question: Which looks darker: black paper, or a small hole into a closed box?
experiments.predict: Look at the black paper. Will the hole look darker, or just the same? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We look at the paper and the hole side by side, in the same light, from the same place. The only difference is that one is paper and one is a hole.

materials.item: a shoebox with its lid, or any small cardboard box that closes
a sheet of black chart paper, or black paper cut from a magazine
glue or tape
a pencil, to make the hole (for a grown-up)
more black paper or a black cloth to line the inside, if you have it

experiments.safety: A grown-up pokes the hole, pushing the pencil away from fingers.

schedule.what: Cover a box with black paper, poke a small hole, and compare the hole with the paper.

experiments.record: Draw the box with its black paper and its hole. Colour the darkest part darkest. Write: the hole is darker because…

setup.art: A shoebox with one side covered by black paper, and a grown-up pushing a pencil through the paper to make a hole the size of a fingertip.
setup.caption: 1. Cover one side with black paper. A grown-up pokes a small hole.

setup.art: A boy in a bright room looking closely at the box, where the small hole is a deeper black than the black paper around it.
setup.caption: 2. Close the lid. Look at the hole and the paper.

flow.do: 1. If you have spare black paper or cloth, line the inside of the box with it. 2. Glue black paper over one outside side of the box. 3. Push a pencil through the middle to make a hole as wide as the pencil. 4. Close the lid.
flow.say: We have covered the box with black paper. Now I will make a small hole in it. Black is the darkest colour we have.
flow.kid: Watch the grown-up make a small hole in the black paper.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess which will look darker, the hole or the black paper around it.
flow.say: Look at the black paper. Now look at the hole. Which one will look darker? Or will they look the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which is darker: the hole or the paper? Why do you think so?
flow.parent: Many children say they will look the same, because both are black.

flow.do: 1. Hold the box near a window or under the room light. 2. Let your child look closely at the hole and the paper from an arm's length. 3. Then from very close.
flow.say: Look carefully. Which is darker? Can you see the surface of the paper? Can you see anything inside the hole?
flow.kid: Look closely. Which is darker? Can you see anything in the hole?

good: The hole.
The hole is blacker than the black paper.

flow.parent: The hole looks clearly darker. Black paper still sends back a little light, so you can see its surface. Light that goes into the hole bounces around inside the closed box and is taken in. Almost none comes back out. If the inside of your box is white, the hole looks less dark, but usually still darker.

flow.do: Ask your child to explain what they saw.
flow.say: Black paper sends back a little light. What about the hole? Why is it so dark?
flow.kid: Why is the hole so dark? Where did the light go?

check.q: Thara, a girl in Mysuru, sees that the hole in her box is darker than black paper. Why?
options: Almost no light comes back out of the hole
Dark is stored in the box
check.why: We see a thing when light comes from it to our eyes. Black paper sends back a little light. Light that goes into the hole is taken in by the inside of the box, so almost none comes back. Where no light comes from, we see darkness.

activities.title: The Door Test: does the dark come out?
activities.context: In this activity you stand in a dark room while a grown-up opens the door to a lit hall. You watch what comes in. Then you swap, and watch whether any dark comes out.

materials.item: a room you can make dark, such as a bathroom, next to a room with the light on
a sheet of white paper

schedule.what: Open a door between a dark room and a lit room, from both sides, and watch.

activities.record: Draw the door, the dark room and the lit room. Draw arrows to show what moved.

setup.art: A girl standing in a dark bathroom, a white sheet of paper on the floor, and a thin line of light at the edge of the door.
setup.caption: 1. Stand in the dark room. Put white paper on the floor.

setup.art: The bathroom door opening, a band of light falling across the floor and the white paper, and the girl watching.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up opens the door slowly. Watch the paper.

setup.art: The girl now standing in the bright hall, looking into the dark bathroom as the door opens, and the hall still bright.
setup.caption: 3. Swap places. Does dark come out into the hall?

flow.do: 1. Switch off the light in a small room, such as the bathroom. 2. Put the white paper on its floor. 3. Your child stands inside. 4. You stand outside in the lit hall and close the door.
flow.say: Stand in the dark room and look at the white paper on the floor. Soon I will open the door. What do you think will happen? Why?
flow.kid: Stand in the dark. Look at the paper. What will happen when the door opens?
flow.parent: If your child is nervous in the dark, go in with them and let them open the door. A little light under the door is fine; a towel along the gap makes it darker.

flow.do: Open the door very slowly, a little at a time.
flow.say: I am opening the door. Watch the paper. What do you see?
flow.kid: Watch the paper as the door opens. What do you see?

good: Light came in.
The paper got brighter as the door opened.

flow.do: Swap places. Your child stands in the lit hall. You go into the dark room and close the door. Then open it slowly.
flow.say: Now you are in the bright hall. When I open the door, will the dark come out into the hall? Watch the floor near the door.
flow.kid: Now you are in the bright hall. Will the dark come out? Watch.

good: No.
The hall stayed bright. The light went into the dark room.

flow.do: Ask your child what they noticed.
flow.say: Light came in through the door. Did dark ever come out? What do you think dark is?
flow.kid: Light came in. Dark never came out. What do you think dark is?

ask.q: What do you think dark is?
good: Where there is no light.
Dark is just no light.

flow.parent: Let your child say it in their own words.

activities.title: Where Is the Sun? Read the bright side of the Moon
activities.context: In this activity you look at the Moon on a few evenings, from a window or a balcony. You draw which side of the Moon is bright, and find where the Sun is.

materials.item: a window or balcony where you can see some of the sky
paper and a pencil

activities.safety: Look at the Moon only after the Sun has set or is hidden. Never look at the Sun itself.

schedule.what: Find the Moon in the evening. Draw its shape and which side is bright. Point to where the Sun went down.
Look again at the same time. Draw it again, then compare the two drawings. Which way did the bright side face each time?

activities.record: Draw the Moon each evening. Draw an arrow from the bright side towards where the Sun went down.

setup.art: A child and a grown-up at a balcony at dusk, the child pointing to a thick crescent Moon, and an orange glow on the horizon where the Sun has set.
setup.caption: 1. Find the Moon in the evening sky.

setup.art: A child's drawing of a half-lit Moon with an arrow from its bright side pointing towards a little sunset drawn on the horizon.
setup.caption: 2. Draw it. Which side is bright? Where is the Sun?

flow.do: 1. In the week after Amavasya, the new Moon, look out after sunset. The Moon will be in the west, near where the Sun set. 2. Help your child find it. 3. Ask them to draw it.
flow.say: Can you find the Moon? Which side of it is bright? Now point to where the Sun went down.
flow.kid: Find the Moon. Which side is bright? Point to where the Sun went down.
flow.parent: A calendar with Amavasya and Purnima marked helps. The thin evening Moon is easiest to see in the first week after Amavasya. If clouds hide the Moon, try another night, or look at a Moon photo taken in the evening.

flow.do: Two days later, look again at the same time. Draw it again.
flow.say: The Moon has moved and grown fatter. Which side is bright now? Is it still the side near the Sun?
flow.kid: Draw the Moon again. Which side is bright now?

flow.do: Put the drawings side by side.
flow.say: Look at your drawings. Which way did the bright side face each time? What does that tell us about where the Moon's light comes from?
flow.kid: Look at your drawings. Which way did the bright side face?

ask.q: Which way did the bright side face?
good: Towards where the Sun went down.
Towards the Sun.

check.q: Ananya, a girl in Lucknow, sees the Moon in the evening. The bright side faces the place where the Sun has just set. What does this show?
options: The Moon's light comes from the Sun
The Moon makes light on one side only
The Sun is behind the Moon
check.why: The bright side of the Moon always faces the Sun, wherever the Sun is. That is because the Moon's light is sunlight bouncing off it.

activities.title: Arrows of Light: draw how moonlight reaches you
activities.context: In this activity you draw a picture that explains: the Sun, the Moon, the Earth and your window. Then you draw arrows to show the path the light takes to your eyes.

materials.item: a big sheet of paper
crayons, with a yellow one

activities.record: Keep the drawing. Write one sentence under it: moonlight is…

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a yellow Sun on the left, a grey Moon at the top and a round Earth on the right with a tiny house and a girl at the window.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the Sun, the Moon and the Earth with your home.

setup.art: The same drawing with yellow arrows from the Sun to the Moon, and from the Moon down to the girl's eyes.
setup.caption: 2. Draw arrows to show where the light goes.

flow.do: Give your child the paper and crayons. Ask them to draw the Sun, the Moon and the Earth with your home on it.
flow.say: Draw the Sun, the Moon and the Earth. Put our home on the Earth, on the side away from the Sun, because it is night there.
flow.kid: Draw the Sun, the Moon and the Earth. Put your home on the night side.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw yellow arrows to show how the light gets to their eyes at night.
flow.say: Where does the light start? Draw an arrow. Where does it go next? Where does it end?
flow.kid: Where does the light start? Draw arrows all the way to your eyes.

good: At the Sun.
The Sun, then the Moon, then my eyes.

flow.parent: A strong drawing has an arrow from the Sun to the Moon, and a second arrow from the Moon to the child. If the arrows start at the Moon, ask: where did the Moon get its light?

flow.do: Ask your child to say one sentence about their drawing.
flow.say: Tell me about your drawing. What is moonlight?
flow.kid: What is moonlight? Say it in your own words.

good: Sunlight that bounced off the Moon.
It is the Sun's light.

games.title: Trace It Back: a card game about where light comes from
games.players: 2 or more players. Take turns to be the reader.
games.context: This is a card game. Each card shows something bright, or something dark. You say where its light started, step by step.

items.b: Sun, then Moon, then the floor.

items.f: A shining steel plate in the kitchen
items.b: Tube light or sunlight, then the plate.

items.f: A bright white wall at noon

items.b: LIGHT SOURCE. The screen makes its own light.

items.f: The Moon in the night sky
A lit diya at Karthigai Deepam
items.b: LIGHT SOURCE. The flame makes its own light.
A lamp or the Sun, then your face, then the mirror.

items.f: A shiny road sign at night
items.b: A car's headlights, then the sign.
LIGHT SOURCE. Fireflies make their own light.
DARK. No light is getting in, so there is nothing to trace.

items.f: A white kolam on the doorstep at dusk
items.b: The evening sky, which is lit by the Sun, then the kolam.

items.f: A wet road shining under a street light
items.b: The street light, then the wet road.

rules: Mix the 12 cards and put them in a pile, face down.
Take turns. On your turn, take the top card and read the front out loud.
Say where its light started, and every place it went on the way. If it is a light source, say 'light source!'. If no light gets there, say 'dark!'.
Another player turns the card over and reads the back. If your answer matches, you keep the card. If not, put it at the bottom of the pile.
When the pile is gone, count your cards. The player with the most cards wins. If you tie, you both win.

setup.art: Twelve cards in a pile on a mat, and a child and a grown-up sitting either side of them.
setup.caption: 1. Put the cards in a pile, face down.

setup.art: A girl holding the card 'Moonlight on the terrace floor', tracing a path in the air with her finger from up high to the floor.
setup.caption: 2. Say where the light started. Another player turns the card to check.

flow.do: Read the rules together. Put the cards face down.
flow.say: Each card shows something bright or dark. You say where its light started, step by step.
flow.kid: Say where the light on each card started.

flow.do: Play until the pile is gone. Read each front, wait for the answer and the reason, then the other player reads the back.
flow.say: Moonlight on the terrace floor. Where did that light start? Where did it go next?
flow.kid: Read the card. Where did its light start? Turn it over.
flow.parent: The Moon cards are the tricky ones. If your child says the light started at the Moon, ask: where did the Moon get it?

flow.do: Count the cards. Then ask about the dark card.
flow.say: Inside a shut dabba, what is there to trace? Why is it dark in there?
flow.kid: Why is it dark inside the shut dabba?

check.q: Sindhu, a girl in Chennai, gets the card 'The Moon in the night sky'. Where did its light start?
check.why: The Moon makes no light of its own. Its light starts at the Sun and bounces off the Moon to us.

games.title: Sun and Moons: a moving game
games.players: 2 or more players: one Sun, and one or more Moons.
games.context: This is a moving game. One player is the Sun. Everyone else is a Moon holding a white plate or a sheet of white paper. A Moon may dance only while the Sun faces the Moon.

items.b: That Moon dances. Any other Moon freezes. Light reaches only that Moon.
All Moons freeze. No light is reaching them.
All Moons dance. It is a full Moon night!

items.f: Hold a book up in front of you, like a cloud, and face the Moons.
items.b: All Moons freeze. The cloud blocks the light.

items.f: Face one Moon, then turn to face a different Moon.
items.b: The first Moon freezes at once. The second Moon starts to dance.

items.f: Face the Moons, then turn your back.
items.b: Dance, then freeze at once. Light stops the moment it stops arriving.

rules: One player is the Sun and holds a yellow paper or cloth. Everyone else is a Moon and holds a white paper plate or a sheet of white paper. With two players, there is one Moon.
The Moons stand around the room, and freeze.
The Sun takes a sky card from the pile, reads the front to themselves, and does what it says. Afterwards, everyone reads the back to check.
A Moon may dance only while the Sun faces that Moon. When the Sun is not facing a Moon, that Moon freezes at once.

A Moon who moves while no light reaches that Moon sits out the next card. After all 6 cards, swap so a new player is the Sun. There is no winner: the aim is to get through all 6 cards without sitting out.

setup.art: A girl holding a yellow paper as the Sun, facing a boy holding a white paper plate who is dancing, while a third child with a plate stands frozen.
setup.caption: 1. The Sun faces a Moon. That Moon shines and dances.

setup.art: The girl turned away, and all the Moon children frozen with their plates.
setup.caption: 2. The Sun turns away. Freeze!

flow.do: Choose the Sun. Give everyone else a white plate or paper. Read the rules. Mix the 6 cards and put them in a pile.
flow.say: The Sun gives light. The Moons give none of their own. A Moon may dance only while the Sun faces them.
flow.kid: Moons, dance only when the Sun faces you!

flow.do: Play all 6 sky cards. Then swap the Sun and play again if there is time.
flow.say: The Sun turns away from you. What do the Moons do? Why?
flow.kid: Watch the Sun. Dance or freeze?

flow.do: Stop and ask the question.
flow.say: Why did the Moons freeze when the Sun turned away?
flow.kid: Why did you freeze when the Sun turned away?

check.q: Lakshmi, a girl playing a Moon, must freeze when the Sun turns away from her. Why?
options: No light reaches her, and Moons make none of their own
The Moon shines only on Sundays
check.why: A Moon has no light of its own. It shines only while sunlight reaches it. When the light stops arriving, it goes dark.

projects.title: The Paper Moon Night-Light
projects.context: In this project you make a big paper Moon and stick it on a wall. At night, you shine a torch on it and use it to light your room softly.

materials.item: a sheet of white chart paper, or a white paper plate
a steel plate or bowl, to draw round
a grey crayon or pencil
scissors (a grown-up helps)
tape
a torch

schedule.what: Make a paper Moon, stick it on the wall, and light the room with it at night.

projects.record: Draw your room lit by your paper Moon, with arrows from the torch to the Moon and on to the room.

setup.art: A girl drawing round a steel plate on white chart paper, and grey crayon craters on a cut-out circle beside her.
setup.caption: 1. Draw round a plate. Cut it out. Add grey craters.

setup.art: A dark bedroom with a white paper Moon taped on the wall, a torch on the bed pointing at it, and soft light falling on a book on the bed.
setup.caption: 2. At night, shine the torch on your Moon. Read by its light.

flow.do: 1. Draw round the steel plate on the white paper. 2. Help your child cut out the circle. 3. They draw a few light grey patches and small round craters.
flow.say: The real Moon has dark patches and craters. Draw some on your Moon. Keep most of it white. Why do we keep it white?
flow.kid: Draw round the plate. Cut it out. Add a few grey craters. Keep most of it white.

ask.q: Why keep most of it white?
good: White sends back the most light.
So it lights the room better.

flow.do: Tape the paper Moon on a wall, a little higher than your child's head.
flow.say: Where shall we put our Moon? Up high, like the real one.
flow.kid: Stick your Moon high on the wall.

flow.do: 1. At night, switch off the room light. 2. Your child shines the torch on the paper Moon, not on the room. 3. They try to see a book or a toy by the Moon's light. 4. Then switch the torch off.
flow.say: Shine your torch on the Moon. Can you see your book? Where does that light come from? Now switch the torch off.
flow.kid: Shine the torch on your Moon. Can you see your book? Now switch it off.

ask.q: What happened when the torch went off?
good: The paper Moon went dark.
The room went dark, because no light reached the Moon.

flow.parent: The light is soft and dim. Hold the book close to the paper Moon, and give your eyes a minute to get used to the dark.

flow.do: Ask the last question.
flow.say: In our room, the torch is the Sun. What is the real Moon's torch?
flow.kid: Your torch is like the Sun. What lights the real Moon?

check.q: Ishita, a girl in Surat, lights her room with a paper Moon and a torch. What is the torch like?
check.why: The torch is the light source, like the Sun. The paper Moon only sends the light on, like the real Moon.

challenges.title: Light the Hidden Picture
challenges.context: This is a problem to solve. A picture is hidden behind a box, and the torch must not move. How can you get light to the picture?
challenges.problem: Meera, a girl in Hyderabad, puts a picture behind a big box in a dark room. The torch is fixed on the other side and shines at the wall. She may not move the torch. How can she light up the picture, the way the Moon lights up the night when the Sun is hidden?
constraints: The torch stays where it is, pointing the same way.
The box stays where it is.
Use only things you already have at home.
materials: a big box or a pile of books
general: Hold a mirror in the torch beam and turn it until the light lands on the picture.
Hold a big white sheet where the beam hits, so it spreads light all round, even behind the box.
creative: Use two mirrors, one after the other, to send the light round the corner.
Crumple a sheet of foil a little and flatten it. Hold it in the beam to send light in a wider patch.
challenges.your_turn: Find two ways to light the hidden picture. Which way made it brightest? Which way lit up the most of the room?

setup.art: A dark room with a torch on the floor shining at a wall, a big box in the middle, and a picture hidden behind the box.
setup.caption: 1. The torch stays still. The picture is hidden behind the box.

setup.art: A girl holding a mirror in the torch beam, tilting it so a bright patch of light lands on the hidden picture.
setup.caption: 2. Use a bouncer to send the light round.

flow.do: Set up the torch, the box and the picture in a dark room. Read the problem.
flow.say: The torch can't move, and the picture is hidden. How can we get light to the picture?
flow.kid: The torch can't move. How can you light the hidden picture?

good: A mirror.
White paper, to bounce the light.

flow.do: Let your child try their ideas. Help only if asked.
flow.say: Try your idea. Can you see the picture? Can you make it brighter?
flow.kid: Try your idea. Can you see the picture now? Try another way.

flow.do: Talk about which way worked best.
flow.say: Which way worked best? Which light source did every way start with?
flow.kid: Which way was best? Where did the light start?

check.q: Meera lit the hidden picture with a mirror. Where did the light on the picture start?
check.why: The mirror makes no light. It only sends on the torch's light. Every way that works starts with a light source.

items.p: A grown-up reads each one. Does it make its own light, or does it only send on light? Colour the light sources yellow.
items.why: The Sun, the tube light and the diya make their own light. The Moon, the wall and the plate only send on light that falls on them.

items.p: Remember the Paper Moon test, where a torch shone on different sheets in the dark. Which sheet let you see the most pictures?
items.why: White paper sends back most of the light that falls on it. Black cloth takes in most of it, and newspaper is in between.

items.p: Draw the Sun, the Moon and your home at night. Draw arrows to show how the light gets to your window.
items.a: An arrow from the Sun to the Moon, and an arrow from the Moon to the home.
items.why: A strong drawing starts the light at the Sun, not at the Moon, and shows the light bouncing off the Moon.
items.art: An empty box with a small sun shape in one corner and a small house in the other.

items.p: A white kolam on a doorstep makes its own light at dusk.
items.why: False. A kolam only sends on light that falls on it from the sky. It is easy to see because white sends back a lot of light.

items.p: Where would it be darkest?
items.why: No light can get into a shut cupboard, so nothing is lit and it is dark. Light passes through glass and a thin sheet.

items.p: Draw a line from each thing to where its light comes from.
items.why: The Moon sends on sunlight, and the page sends on lamplight. The diya makes its own light.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: in the Door Test, light came into the dark room. Why did no dark come out into the hall?
items.a: Dark is not a thing that can move. It is only where light is not arriving. Light moves out from a light source.
items.why: A strong answer says that dark is no light, so there is nothing to come out.

items.p: Darkness is what we see where no ____ is arriving.
items.why: Darkness is the absence of light.

items.p: Kavya, aged 7, and her cousin Arjun, aged 5, look at the full Moon from their terrace in Madurai.

views.says: The Moon is the brightest thing in the night sky, so it must be a light source.
The Moon is bright, but its light comes from the Sun.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason from your own tests. Then say what Arjun noticed that is true.
items.a: Kavya is right about where the light starts. Arjun is right that the Moon is very bright at night.
items.why: A strong answer uses evidence, such as the white paper going dark when the torch went off, or the bright side facing the Sun. It also says fairly that Arjun's noticing is true: the Moon really is bright.

items.p: Look at this street at night. Count only the light sources. Write the number.
items.why: There are 4 light sources: a street light, a lit window, a scooter headlight and a star. The Moon, the shiny car roof and the white wall only send on light.
items.art: A street at night with one street light, one lit window, a scooter with its headlight on, one star, the Moon, a shiny car roof and a white wall.

items.p: Why did the black cloth light up fewer pictures than the white paper? Say it, and a grown-up writes it.
items.a: The black cloth takes in most of the torch's light and sends back very little. The white paper sends back most of it.
items.why: A strong answer says what each sheet does with the light, not just that one is black.

items.p: Three of these shine only with light from somewhere else. Which one makes its own light? Circle it.
items.why: Fireflies make light inside their bodies. The Moon, the mirror and the kolam only send on light.

items.p: Look at the picture of the Sun, the Moon and the Earth. Write 'bright' or 'dark' on each half of the Moon.
items.why: The half of the Moon that faces the Sun is lit. The half facing away gets no sunlight, so it is dark.
items.art: The Sun on the left, the Moon in the middle with two empty labels on its two halves, and the Earth on the right.

items.p: If you wait long enough in a room with no light at all, your eyes will get used to it and you will see.
items.why: False. Eyes get used to dim light, not to no light. With no light at all, nothing can come from the things to your eyes.

items.p: On a dark road, why is a person in a white shirt easier to see than a person in a black shirt?
opts: The white shirt sends back more of the light that falls on it
The white shirt makes its own light
The black shirt makes the road darker
items.why: White sends back most of the light that falls on it, as the white paper did in the Paper Moon test. Black takes most of it in.

items.p: Put the journey of moonlight in order, from start to end.
items: It bounces off the grey rock
a: It bounces off the grey rock
items.why: Moonlight starts at the Sun, travels to the Moon, bounces off its rock and comes down to us.

items.p: In a power cut, Kavya's Amma, her Paati and her friend Farhan, aged 8, talk about what darkness is.

views.says: Darkness is nothing. It is only where light is missing.
Darkness is real. I can see it and feel it all around me.
Darkness comes in when the lights go off, like water flowing in.

items.ask: Which idea fits the Door Test best? Give a reason. Then say one thing about another idea that makes sense.
items.a: Amma's idea fits the door test best: light came in, and no dark ever came out. Paati is right that we really do see the dark. Farhan's idea does not fit, because nothing came in when the lights went off.
items.why: A strong answer uses the door test as evidence. People in India argued about this long ago: some schools said darkness is only missing light, and Jain thinkers counted it as something real.

items.p: A cloud covers the Moon, and the terrace goes dark. Where did the dark come from? Say it, and a grown-up writes it.
items.a: The dark did not come from anywhere. The cloud blocked the moonlight, so light stopped arriving on the terrace.
items.why: A strong answer says what changed: the light stopped arriving. Nothing dark arrived.

items.p: Draw the box from the Blackest Black test. Colour the hole and the black paper. Make the darker one darker.
items.a: The hole is coloured darker than the black paper.
items.why: Black paper sends back a little light. Almost no light comes back out of the hole, so it looks darkest.

items.p: Leela, a girl in Pune, sees the Moon in the daytime. It looks pale and faint. Why?
opts: The sky around it is bright too
The Moon makes less light in the day
items.why: The Moon reflects the same sunlight all the time. At night the sky around it is black, so it looks bright. In the day the sky is bright too, so the Moon looks pale.

items.p: Many people think the Moon gives light because it is so bright at night. What could you look at to show them where its light comes from? Say it, and a grown-up writes it.
items.a: Look at which side of the Moon is bright: it always faces where the Sun is or where it set. Or show them the Paper Moon test, where the paper went dark when the torch went off.
items.why: A strong answer names something you can really see or do, not just 'a book says so'.

items.p: Moon rock is dark grey. It reflects only about one tenth of the sunlight that falls on it. Why can the Moon still light up a terrace?
opts: The Moon stores light in the day
items.why: Sunlight is so strong that even one tenth of it, bounced off the Moon, is enough to see by at night.

items.p: Two friends in Kolkata, Rimi and Joy, test bouncers in the dark.

views.says: The foil is the best bouncer, because it is the shiniest.
The white paper is the best, because it showed the most pictures.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Can they both be right? Use what you saw in the Paper Moon test.
items.a: Both can be right in different ways. Foil sends light in one direction, so it makes a very bright patch where it points. White paper spreads light everywhere, so it lights the whole card more evenly.
items.why: A strong answer sees that 'best' depends on what you want: one bright spot, or light spread all round.

items.p: Divya, a girl in Bhopal, says on a moonlit night: the Sun is lighting my floor. Is she right? Explain. Say it, and a grown-up writes it.
items.a: Yes. Moonlight is sunlight that bounced off the Moon. So the light on her floor started at the Sun, about eight minutes earlier.
items.why: A strong answer traces the light back to the Sun and says the Moon only sends it on.

items.p: Sort these into 'makes light' and 'only sends light on'.
items: A cat's eyes shining in a torch beam
items.why: Lightning, glow-worms and stars make their own light. A cat's eyes and a bicycle reflector shine only when light falls on them.

items.p: If the Sun suddenly stopped shining, what would happen to the Moon about eight minutes later?
items.why: Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach the Moon. After that, no more light would arrive, so the Moon would have nothing to send on.

items.p: Draw a picture that shows darkness. Then write: how did you show it, when darkness is no light?
items.a: Any honest drawing, for example a black shut cupboard, with a sentence like: I drew no light reaching inside.
items.why: A strong answer sees that we draw darkness by leaving out light, or by showing that light is blocked.

items.p: This is the Paper Moon test from above. Label the light source, the bouncer and the thing being lit.
items.why: The torch makes the light. The white paper sends it on. The picture card is lit by the bounced light, the way the Earth is lit by the Moon.

items.p: Moonlight is sunlight that has ____ off the Moon.
items.why: The Moon makes no light. Sunlight bounces off its grey rock and comes down to us.

items.p: Astronauts on the Moon saw that its ground is bright white, like snow.
items.why: False. Moon rock and dust are dark grey. The Moon looks white from Earth because sunlight is strong and the night sky is dark.

quiz.p: Which of these is a light source?
quiz.why: A tube light makes its own light. The Moon and a mirror only send on light from somewhere else.

quiz.p: Which of these only sends on light and makes none of its own?
quiz.why: A diya and a tube light make their own light. A white wall only sends on light that falls on it.

quiz.p: Where does the Moon's light come from?
quiz.why: The Moon is a ball of rock. Sunlight bounces off it and comes to us.

quiz.p: What is the Moon made of?
quiz.why: Astronauts brought back Moon rock and dust. They are dark grey and make no light.

quiz.p: Which side of the Moon is bright?
quiz.why: Sunlight falls on the side facing the Sun, so that side is bright. The other side is dark.

quiz.p: Priya, a girl in Indore, shines a torch on white paper in the dark. The paper lights up her drawing. What is the paper like?
quiz.why: The paper sends on the torch's light, the way the Moon sends on the Sun's light.

quiz.p: Which sheet sends back the least torch light?
quiz.why: Black cloth takes in most of the light that falls on it, so it sends back the least.

opts: A black gas that fills rooms
quiz.why: Darkness is the absence of light. Where no light arrives, we see dark.

quiz.p: In the Paper Moon test, why did we keep the torch and the card in the same places?
opts: So only the sheet changed, to make the test fair
So the pictures would not move
quiz.why: In a fair test, we change only one thing. Then we know the sheet made the difference.

quiz.p: Why must you never look straight at the Sun?
opts: It can hurt your eyes for ever
It makes the Sun go out
quiz.why: The Sun is far brighter than any other light source we have. Looking straight at it can damage your eyes, and the damage may not heal.

videos.title: Earthshine: the dark part of a crescent Moon glowing faintly
videos.why: Shows sunlight bouncing off the Earth, then off the Moon, lighting the Moon's dark part. It fits Leonardo da Vinci's idea in the story of how we found out.
videos.check: Find a real photo or video of earthshine on a thin crescent Moon, from a space agency or an astronomy channel. Check it says the glow is sunlight reflected by the Earth.

videos.title: Chandrayaan-3 on the Moon: pictures of the grey ground
videos.why: Shows that the Moon's ground is grey rock and dust, lit by the Sun, with sharp black shadows.
videos.check: Find an ISRO clip of the Vikram lander or Pragyan rover pictures from August 2023. Check that it shows the real ground, not an animation.

videos.title: A full Moon rising over the sea, sped up
videos.why: Shows how bright the Moon looks against the dark sky, and moonlight on the water.
videos.check: Find a real time-lapse of a moonrise, ideally over the sea at Chennai, Puri or Kanyakumari. Check it is not edited to make the Moon bigger.

applications: Road signs and the stripes on police jackets are made to reflect car headlights back to drivers, so they shine at night with no light of their own.
White walls and ceilings make a room brighter, because they reflect lamp light all around. Many homes in hot places are painted white for this, and to stay cooler.

ISRO's Chandrayaan spacecraft photograph the Moon's ground by the sunlight that bounces off it. Chandrayaan-2 had two women at its head: project director M. Vanitha and mission director Ritu Karidhal.
Photographers use a white sheet called a reflector to bounce sunlight onto a person's face and fill in the shadows.

spotted.text: At Sharad Purnima in many parts of India, families leave kheer or milk out in the light of the full Moon. That moonlight is sunlight bounced off the Moon.
spotted.art: A bowl of kheer on a terrace wall at night, lit by a full Moon.

spotted.text: On Onam nights in Kerala, white flowers in the pookalam are easier to see in dim light than dark red ones.
spotted.art: A round pookalam of flowers at dusk, its white flowers standing out and its red flowers looking dark.

spotted.text: Reflective stripes on a Mumbai bus or a Kolkata taxi flash brightly in car headlights.
spotted.art: A bus at night with shining reflective stripes caught in a car's headlights.

spotted.text: In a power cut in Chennai, a phone torch pointed at the white ceiling lights up the whole room.
spotted.art: A family in a dark room with a phone torch pointing up, and a soft patch of light on the white ceiling lighting everyone.

spotted.text: On a full-Moon night by the Brahmaputra in Assam, moonlight makes a silver path on the water.
spotted.art: A wide river at night with a silver band of moonlight across the water and a small boat.

open_questions.q: How exactly did the Moon form?
open_questions.why_open: Most scientists think a planet-sized body crashed into the young Earth, and the Moon formed from the pieces. But some Moon rocks are so like Earth rocks that scientists still argue about how it happened.

open_questions.q: How much water ice is hidden in the dark craters at the Moon's poles?
open_questions.why_open: Some craters near the Moon's poles never get sunlight, so they stay dark and very cold. Chandrayaan-1 helped find water on the Moon, but nobody knows yet how much ice these dark craters hold.

open_questions.q: Is darkness something, or only nothing?
open_questions.why_open: Physics says darkness is the absence of light. But thinkers in India and elsewhere argued about it for centuries, and philosophers still ask whether an absence can be a real thing.

ask_kids: Is the Moon out tonight? Which side of it is bright?
Which things in this room make their own light? Which only send light on?
Why is it dark inside a closed cupboard?
Where is the Sun right now, while it is night here?
Which shirt would help a person be seen at night: a white one or a black one? Why?
When you shut your eyes, is it dark? Where did the light go?

jokes.j: Why did the Moon skip dinner?
What did the Moon say to the Sun?
jokes.a: Thanks for the light. I'll pass it on!

jokes.j: Why was the black cloth so warm?
jokes.a: It kept all the light to itself!

jokes.j: How do you catch darkness in a jar?
jokes.a: You can't. Open the lid, and the light gets in first!

jokes.j: Why did the white paper get a prize?
Why is the Moon never lonely at night?
jokes.a: The Sun keeps sending it light!

jokes.j: What did the torch say to the paper Moon?
How does the Moon cut its hair?

maths.problem: In the Paper Moon test, Gayathri, a girl in Coimbatore, saw 6 pictures with white paper and 2 with newspaper. How many more did the white paper show?
maths.explain: Count on from 2 to 6: 3, 4, 5, 6. That is 4. So the white paper showed 4 more pictures than the newspaper.
maths.context: This is about the Paper Moon test, where you counted pictures lit by bounced light.
maths.why_maths: Finding the difference shows how much better one sheet is than another, not just which one wins.

maths.problem: Mona, a girl in Nagpur, wrote down these made-up results: white paper 6, foil 4, newspaper 3, black cloth 1. Put the sheets in order from most pictures to fewest.
maths.answer: White paper, foil, newspaper, black cloth.
maths.explain: 6 is the biggest, then 4, then 3, then 1. So the order is white paper, foil, newspaper, black cloth.
maths.context: This is about the Paper Moon test, with made-up results.
maths.why_maths: Putting the results in order shows the pattern at a glance: the paler the sheet, the more pictures we see.

maths.problem: Sneha, a girl in Jaipur, did the Paper Moon test, but her black cloth showed 5 pictures, nearly as many as white paper. Her friend says a little light was coming under the door. What would you change, and why?
maths.answer: Put a towel along the gap under the door, then test again.
maths.explain: Light from under the door was lighting the pictures too, so the count was not only from the bounced light. Blocking it makes the test fair.
maths.context: This is about the Paper Moon test, and a result that looked odd.
maths.why_maths: An odd number in a result is a clue that something else changed, and finding it makes the test fair.

maths.problem: Revathi, a girl in Kochi, sees the full Moon rise at 6 o'clock in the evening. She watches it until 8 o'clock. For how many hours did she watch?
maths.explain: From 6 to 7 is 1 hour. From 7 to 8 is 1 more hour. So she watched for 2 hours.
maths.context: This is about watching the Moon in the evening.
maths.why_maths: Counting the hours between two times helps us plan how long to watch the sky.

roots.context: We have made a paper Moon in the dark and watched light come in through a door. Now we ask what that tells us about the night, about ourselves and about the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the dark room, the white paper lit your pictures only while the torch shone on it. The Moon lights our nights the same way, with sunlight. So on a moonlit night, the light on your floor left the Sun about eight minutes earlier.
deep_truth.habit: We split time into day, when the Sun lights us, and night, when the Sun is gone. Moonlight shows that the Sun keeps lighting our nights, by way of the Moon.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Paper Moon test, the pictures went dark the moment the torch went off. The bright side of the Moon always faces the Sun, and Moon rock makes no light of its own.

three.who_am_i: You see only what light reaches you. Almost everything you see, you see by light that bounced off it.
three.what_is_life: On full-Moon nights, many sea creatures, such as some corals, time their lives by moonlight. They are living by sunlight that came the long way round.
three.what_is_this_world: The world has a few light sources and countless things that pass light on. The Moon, the walls of your home and your own face all pass on light.

roots.thread: The Sun makes the light, and the Moon, the clouds, the walls and your face pass it on. The light on your terrace floor is the Sun's light, bounced once off the Moon. Everything is aware in its own way, the Sun and the Moon too. Many scientists disagree, and say only living beings with nerves are aware.

teachings.teaching: There the Sun does not shine, nor the Moon and the stars. Everything shines only after that one light shines. By its light, all this is lit.
teachings.link: In the Paper Moon test, the paper shone only after the torch shone. In the sky, the Moon shines only after the Sun. The Upanishad speaks of one light behind all lights, and the paper and the Moon are a small everyday example of shining by another's light.

teachings.teaching: We shape clay into a pot, but it is the empty space inside that makes it useful.
teachings.link: Darkness is an absence, the way the inside of a pot is empty. Yet we notice it, name it and use it, for example to sleep or to see the stars.

science.text: The Moon makes no light of its own. It reflects about one tenth of the sunlight that falls on it.
Darkness is the absence of light. Even outer space between the stars is not perfectly dark: a faint glow of microwaves from the early universe fills it, and our eyes cannot see it.

other_view.who: Many scientists today, and the old Charvaka school of India
other_view.view: They say the Sun and the Moon are not aware of anything. To them the Moon is only rock, and moonlight is only light bouncing off it. They think awareness belongs to living beings with nerves or brains.

practice.title: Trace the light
practice.say: Sit still in a dim room at night, with one small light on somewhere. Breathe in slowly and out slowly, three times. Now look at the dimmest thing you can still see. Ask yourself where its light started. Follow it back in your mind, from the thing to the lamp, or from the thing to the Moon to the Sun. Breathe out slowly.
practice.kid: Sit still in a dim room. Breathe slowly three times. Look at the dimmest thing you can see. Where did its light start?

ask: Could you see anything at all if nothing ever passed light on?
Is darkness something, or nothing? How would you know?

how_we_found_out.story: Long ago, some thinkers said the Moon works like a smooth, polished mirror, sending sunlight straight back to us. About a thousand years ago, in Cairo, the scientist Ibn al-Haytham, who was born in Basra in what is now Iraq, wrote a book called On the Light of the Moon. He pointed out a problem. A mirror lit by the Sun shows only one small, dazzling spot. But the Moon glows over its whole face. So he argued that every part of the Moon sends sunlight out in all directions, not like a mirror at all. Many people also thought the faint glow on the dark part of a thin crescent Moon was the Moon's own light. Around 1510, Leonardo da Vinci in Italy wrote that this glow is sunlight bounced off the Earth, and then off the Moon. In 1610, Galileo Galilei looked at the Moon through his telescope. He saw bright points in the dark part, just beyond the edge of the light. He worked out that they were mountain tops catching sunlight first, like hilltops on Earth at sunrise. So the Moon is rough rock, lit by the Sun.
how_we_found_out.who: Ibn al-Haytham, a scientist born in Basra who worked in Cairo; Leonardo da Vinci, an Italian artist and inventor; Galileo Galilei, an Italian scientist
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought the Moon was a smooth mirror, and that it gave some faint light of its own. Ibn al-Haytham showed it is not a mirror, and Leonardo and Galileo showed that all its light comes from the Sun.

founder: ideas/by_topic/light-seeing-and-shadows.md: the founder's ideas of using mirrors to bounce light into dark corners and moonlight reflected off water grew into the Paper Moon test, the Hidden Picture challenge and the Brahmaputra spotted card. Her trataka idea was used at Level 1, so this unit's practice is tracing the light instead. Her deeper ideas (photons, the speed of light, the dark box) belong to the Level 3 light units.

Curriculum entry sci.light.light-sources.L2, with Cambridge Primary Science Stage 2, 5.1 Light sources and 5.2 Darkness. This unit leads on from Level 1, where the child found which things make their own light, to the Moon as a reflector and darkness as the absence of light.
science: The Moon's albedo is about 0.11 to 0.12: it reflects roughly a tenth of the sunlight falling on it, similar to worn asphalt. Full moonlight is roughly 400,000 times fainter than sunlight (apparent magnitude about -12.7 against -26.7).
Light takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds from the Sun to the Earth or Moon, and about 1.3 seconds from the Moon to the Earth.

Ibn al-Haytham, Maqala fi daw' al-qamar (On the Light of the Moon), about 1020 to 1030: argued that the Moon does not reflect like a mirror, since a mirror would show only an image of the Sun. Later readers describe his account as diffuse reflection (H. Salih, UNESCO). The exact wording and date should be checked against a scholarly edition.

Leonardo da Vinci, Codex Leicester (about 1506 to 1510): earthshine explained as sunlight reflected from the Earth. Galileo Galilei, Sidereus Nuncius (1610): bright points beyond the terminator are mountain tops lit by the rising Sun.
Nyaya-Vaisheshika held darkness (tamas) to be the absence of light. Tattvartha Sutra 5.24 lists darkness (tamas) and shadow (chaya) among the modes of matter (pudgala).
Chandrayaan-1's Moon Mineralogy Mapper helped detect water and hydroxyl on the Moon's surface (Pieters and others, Science, 2009). Chandrayaan-3 landed near the Moon's south pole on 23 August 2023.

Katha Upanishad 5.15 (2.2.15), also Mundaka Upanishad 2.2.10: 'na tatra suryo bhati na chandra-tarakam... tam eva bhantam anubhati sarvam'. Tao Te Ching, chapter 11, on the use of empty space in a pot.
Cosmic microwave background: faint radiation from the early universe fills space, at microwave wavelengths that our eyes cannot see.

playtest: Walked through every step as a parent and child in a flat. Both card games now work with two players: Trace It Back has turns, a reader and an ending, and Sun and Moons has 6 cards that all do something, one Sun and any number of Moons. The Paper Moon test now uses a thick pen so the pictures can be seen, and says honestly that foil held flat may send the beam straight back. The Moon-watching schedule matches its steps (day 1 and day 3), the creative idea that moved the torch was removed, names are introduced, repeated questions and one inaccurate joke were cut, and family assumptions and a stock line were taken out.
